newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toshiba says chip market outlook still cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Toshiba says chip market outlook still cloudy.

text.p: The outlook for the semiconductor market is still cloudy and recovery may be delayed until mid-1997, despite a rise in a chip market indicator, a top executive of Japan's Toshiba Corp said on Thursday.

But a sudden boost in chip demand is possible as personal computer (PC) makers, the biggest buyers of chips, have already cut their inventories to a minimum, said Susumu Kohyama, deputy group executive of Toshiba's semiconductor group.
"A wait-and-see stance is prevailing in the industry," Kohyama said in an interview.
He said overall inventories at chip makers, PC makers and distributors were gradually decreasing, but slower than expected PC sales still clouded the outlook of the market.
"A feeling that supply and demand has struck a balance has yet to emerge," Kohyama said, adding that inventories were still not low enough at some chip makers.

He was not elated by a slight rise in a key indicator of semiconductor demand, the book-to-bill ratio, announced on Wednesday. "It's an indicator that shows the trend in the past," Kohyama said. "We hope to be able to read the market trend to the end of this year."
The ratio, compiled by the U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association, measures new chip orders against sales. It rose to 0.90 in August from a revised 0.86 in July, helped by an inching up in orders.
The rise prompted some U.S. analysts to believe an inventory correction is ending and PC orders are accelerating.
Semiconductor makers are waiting to see Christmas season sales of PCs as a future indicator for the chip market.

"We are particularly interested to see how PCs with Microsoft Corp's Windows NT operating software installed will do," said Kohyama. "If Christmas sales are disappointing, an adjustment phase will continue into early or mid-1997."
Sales of Windows NT, used in computer servers, are seen accelerating if companies boost investment in corporate network systems, which comprise PCs and servers.
Following a glut in computer chips, particularly memory chips, Japanese chip makers have scaled back expansion plans or revised earnings forecasts for the year to next March 31.
Industry analysts say Toshiba is relatively bullish in its earnings outlook in the semiconductor division.

The company said earlier it expects the division's current profit to fall only about 50 percent, despite a more than 70 percent plunge in prices of mainstream 16-megabit dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) in the past nine months.
"Higher sales of logic chips will help, although that alone will not be enough to offset lower memory sales," Kohyama said.
Analysts said royalty income from a Taiwanese licensee of Toshiba's memory production know-how will help profits.
Toshiba said earlier it would provide production technology for 64-megabit DRAMs to Taiwan's Winbond Electronics Corp.
